opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think that's really at the core of how Nvidia operates. We see ourselves as a platform company more than a company that just sells chips. If you look at the history, the GPU only became valuable because people built amazing things on top of it: researchers training neural networks, game developers, scientists running simulations. So our success depends on the ecosystem's success. If our partners and customers don't succeed, we don't succeed.

In practice, that means we do a lot of work that isn't directly "selling a product." We build the software stack, CUDA, the libraries, the frameworks, so developers don't have to reinvent everything. We release models and tools, often openly, so people have a strong starting point. In my own area, generative AI and world models for physical AI, a big part of our thinking is: robotics and autonomous vehicle companies need world models, but training one from scratch is extremely expensive and needs huge amounts of data and compute. Not every company can afford that. So we try to build foundation models that people can take and post-train for their own applications, their own robots, their own environments.

There's also a mindset piece. Jensen often says we want to do things that are very hard and that others either can't do or wouldn't do. If something is going to happen anyway without us, we probably shouldn't spend our energy there. We'd rather find the problems where, if we don't push, the whole field moves slower. Then we lay the foundation and let the ecosystem build the many applications on top.

So for me, "helping customers succeed" isn't a slogan. It's a strategy: grow the pie for everyone, and Nvidia grows along with it.

r001.rationale: The response describes Nvidia as a platform company whose success depends on its ecosystem, but does not connect this to early reliance on other companies to manufacture GPU cards.

r002.rationale: It says partners and customers must succeed and that Nvidia aims to grow the pie, but does not state that partners must be able to profit.

r003.rationale: The response discusses building software and models for the ecosystem, but does not explain that customer success on Nvidia’s GPU platform creates more opportunities for those customers to use Nvidia GPUs.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because it's really the core of how we operate. At Nvidia, we don't see ourselves as just a chip company or even just a platform company. Jensen often says that we're in the business of building the infrastructure that other people build on. And when you frame it that way, the success of our customers and partners isn't a nice-to-have, it's literally the measure of whether we've done our job.

Let me give you a concrete example from my own work. When we started building Cosmos, our world foundation model platform for physical AI, we made a deliberate decision early on to open it up. We released the model weights, the tokenizers, the data curation pipeline, the guardrails. Some people asked why we would give that away. But the reasoning is simple. Physical AI, whether it's robotics or autonomous vehicles or industrial automation, is an enormously hard problem, and no single company, not even Nvidia, is going to solve all of it alone. If a robotics startup in Shenzhen or a research lab in Toronto can take Cosmos and fine-tune it for their domain, build something that works, and then they need our compute to scale it, everyone wins. The ecosystem grows, and we grow with it.

I think there's also a deeper cultural piece. Internally there's this phrase about being a "builder of builders." When I talk to a customer, I'm not trying to figure out how to sell them more GPUs this quarter. I'm trying to understand what's actually blocking them. Is it data? Is it simulation fidelity? Is it the gap between what works in a lab demo and what works in a factory at three in the morning? And then we go back and ask what we need to build, as a full stack, so that the next person who hits that wall doesn't have to. That's why we invest so heavily in things like Omniverse, Isaac, the CUDA libraries, all of it. The hardware is the foundation, but the commitment is to the whole stack, because that's what it takes for someone to actually succeed.

And honestly, this is a long game. Jensen talks about CUDA taking fifteen years before it really paid off. We're willing to be patient because we're betting on the ecosystem, not on any one product cycle. If our partners succeed, the market expands, and a bigger market is better for everyone, including us. I genuinely believe that's not just a slogan. It's how we make decisions every day.

astra-6.text:
I think Nvidia’s commitment is about recognizing that our success depends on our customers and partners being successful. It’s not enough to deliver a powerful chip. You also need the software, the tools, and the support that help people turn that computing power into something useful.

That requires listening closely. What are they trying to accomplish? Where are they getting stuck? Sometimes the answer is better performance, but sometimes it’s making a technology easier to adopt or helping solve an engineering problem. To me, that’s what being an ecosystem partner means: working together so that others can build and succeed on the platform.

That means investing in software, tools, and support so people can build, deploy, and succeed with it. Ultimately, Nvidia succeeds when the people building on its platform succeed, so that commitment has to be a long-term partnership.
